Roberto, before we talk about volumes, tell me what you expect from this category in three years.
I think the whole category will grow slowly, and the premium segment will grow fast. That is my opinion, not a plan.
Why premium? Our numbers say consumption per person is flat.
Flat in volume, yes. But people are buying less and paying more for it. Habits are shifting, and that is a trend, not one good year.
All right. And what have you already decided?
We are going to enter the premium segment next year. That one is decided. We are not going to touch the low end.
Your biggest competitor entered it two years ago and took four points of market share. You are late.
We are late, and I will not pretend we are not. But demand is going to grow faster than one company can serve, so there is still an opportunity.

Before you all start arguing, let me give you the two numbers that matter, and then one warning. Over the last four years, volume per person in this category was flat. Almost exactly zero growth, four years running. In the same four years, the money people spend on the category grew nineteen percent. Those two numbers together tell you one story and only one: people are buying less and paying more for what they buy. They moved to smaller packs and to better products, and they did it slowly, in every region we measured, which is what makes it a trend and not a good year. Now the warning, and I want it in the minutes. A trend of four years is not a promise. If income falls, the same people go back to the large cheap pack in one quarter. I have watched it happen twice. So plan for the trend, but do not build a factory that only works if it continues.

People ask me how I decide when to move on something like this, and the honest answer is that I have a rule now because I got it wrong once. First, I separate a trend from a fashion. A trend survives a bad year. A fashion does not: the moment money gets tight, it disappears, and you are left holding a line nobody wants. That test takes about ten minutes with the right data. Second, and this is the part that cost me, I do not wait for certainty. I waited once. I wanted to be sure, and by the time I was sure, two competitors were already inside the segment, and it cost us three times more to enter than it would have cost two years earlier. Three times. So the rule I use today is simple, and I will say it slowly. Enter small and early rather than big and late. A small bet on a real trend beats a large bet on a certain one, because by the time it is certain, you are not early, you are just expensive.
